841.quote_or_event: “No one respects the poor man. … Says Kabir, he alone is poor, who does not have the Naam, the Name of the Lord, in his heart.”
841.explanation: Kabir starts from the world's contempt for the poor and turns it round: the only real poverty is lacking the Name in one's heart.
841.tie_back: The Kural says the lack of understanding is the real poverty and the world should not count other lacks as want; Kabir likewise moves true poverty from money to the inner life.
841.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1159, Raag Bhairao, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
841._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one in structure; for Kabir the missing wealth is the Naam, where the Kural speaks of understanding (arivu).

842.quote_or_event: “He Himself is the Creator, and He Himself is the Enjoyer; He Himself gives, and causes others to give.”
842.explanation: In a pauri of Bihaagre Ki Vaar, Guru Ram Das says that God is the real Giver and is the one who moves others to give.
842.tie_back: The Kural explains a fool's glad giving by the receiver's merit, not the giver's virtue; Gurbani likewise traces any gift beyond the human giver, to God who causes others to give.
842.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 554, Raag Bihaagraa, Bihaagre Ki Vaar (pauri 15), Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
842._accuracy_note: Next-best: both look past the giver for the cause of a gift, but the Kural credits the receiver's past merit (karma) while Gurbani credits God's grace.

843.quote_or_event: “Dadda: Do not blame anyone else; blame instead your own actions. Whatever I did, for that I have suffered; I do not blame anyone else.”
843.explanation: In his acrostic Patti, Guru Nanak teaches that the suffering one meets comes from one's own deeds, not from others.
843.tie_back: The Kural says fools hurt themselves more than any enemy could; Guru Nanak likewise finds the source of suffering in one's own actions, not in others.
843.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 433, Raag Aasaa, Patti Likhi, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
843._accuracy_note: Strong on self-caused suffering; Guru Nanak speaks of everyone's actions, not specifically the fool's, and does not compare it with what enemies do.

844.quote_or_event: “O Nanak! Everyone speaks of Him, each one wiser than the rest. … O Nanak! One who claims to know everything shall not be decorated in the world hereafter.”
844.explanation: In Japji Sahib Guru Nanak notes that everyone holds forth as wiser than the next, and warns that whoever claims to know everything will not be honoured hereafter.
844.tie_back: The Kural defines folly as the conceit that says 'we are the wise ones'; Guru Nanak likewise names the claim to know everything as the mark that disgraces.
844.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 5, Japji Sahib (pauri 21), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
844._accuracy_note: Strong on conceit about one's wisdom as itself folly; Japji speaks of claims to know God's measure, a spiritual rather than general setting.

845.quote_or_event: “O Nanak! The blind man may go to appraise the jewels, but he will not know their value; he will return home after exposing his ignorance.”
845.explanation: In Ramkali Ki Vaar Guru Angad describes the blind man who sets himself up to value jewels and only shows how little he knows.
845.tie_back: The Kural says pretending to know what you never learned destroys your credibility; Guru Angad's blind appraiser exposes his own ignorance the same way.
845.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 954, Raag Raamkalee, Ramkali Ki Vaar (salok 1 before pauri 15), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
845._accuracy_note: Very close on pretence exposing ignorance; the Kural adds that doubt spreads even to one's real skills, which the salok does not say.

846.quote_or_event: “What should I account as the rewards of this human life, if one does not feel love and devotion to the Lord? Wearing clothes and eating food is useless, if the mind is filled with the love of duality.”
846.explanation: Guru Nanak says that the outward routines of life, even dressing and eating, are worthless while the mind remains full of duality.
846.tie_back: The Kural calls it foolish to cover the body carefully while leaving one's faults uncured; Guru Nanak likewise says wearing clothes is useless when the mind is not set right.
846.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1411, Saloks Vaaran Te Vadheek (salok 11), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
846._accuracy_note: Reasonable parallel: both put outer covering beneath inner reform, though Guru Nanak's concern is devotion and duality, not moral faults as such.

847.quote_or_event: “Take the Guru’s advice, you ignorant fool; without devotion, even the clever have drowned.”
847.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib Guru Arjan tells the ignorant to take the Guru's counsel, warning that even clever people sink without it.
847.tie_back: The Kural says the fool who lets precious counsel slip does great harm to himself; Guru Arjan urges the fool to hold fast to the Guru's advice for the same reason.
847.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 288, Raag Gauri, Sukhmani Sahib (ashtapadi 19, stanza 6), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
847._accuracy_note: Fits the reading of the Kural as ignoring precious advice; the other traditional reading, failing to keep a secret, has no parallel here.

848.quote_or_event: “One whom the Lord has made blind - the Lord can make him see again. He acts only as he knows, although he may be spoken to a hundred times.”
848.explanation: In Ramkali Ki Vaar Guru Angad describes a person who goes on acting by his own lights even when told a hundred times, until God opens his eyes.
848.tie_back: The Kural speaks of the one who will not do right even when told and cannot work it out himself; Guru Angad's man who ignores a hundred warnings is the same case.
848.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 954, Raag Raamkalee, Ramkali Ki Vaar (salok 2 before pauri 16), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
848._accuracy_note: Very close on not heeding instruction; Gurbani leaves hope that grace can cure this blindness, where the Kural calls it a disease lasting until death.

849.quote_or_event: “I do not understand myself, and yet I try to teach others. Such is the guide I am! O Nanak! The one who is blind shows others the way, and misleads all his companions.”
849.explanation: In Majh Ki Vaar Guru Nanak, speaking humbly in his own voice, describes the guide who lacks understanding yet teaches others and leads them astray.
849.tie_back: The Kural says the fool shows others only what he himself saw and remains one who never saw the truth; Guru Nanak's blind guide does the same.
849.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 140, Raag Majh, Majh Ki Vaar (salok 2 before pauri 6), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
849._accuracy_note: Fits Puliyur Kesigan's reading of the Kural; the more common reading, that the teacher of a fool ends up looking foolish, is not in this salok.

850.quote_or_event: “Kabir! Do not associate with the faithless cynics; run far away from them. If you touch a vessel stained with soot, some of the soot will stick to you.”
850.explanation: Kabir tells the seeker to keep well away from the saakat, the faithless cynic who turns from God, since such company stains like soot.
850.tie_back: The Kural says one who denies what the wise affirm is set apart like a demon; Kabir likewise sets the faithless cynic apart and tells the seeker to keep away.
850.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1371, Salok Bhagat Kabir (salok 131) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
850._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: both shun the one who rejects accepted truth, but Kabir gives no demon image and his concern is the seeker's own purity.
